think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 44-year-old hypertensive male smoker presents with acute high-grade fever, retro-orbital/frontal headache, myalgias, and coffee-ground emesis, rapidly deteriorating into hypotensive shock (89/52 mmHg), biventricular failure with pulmonary edema, an S3 gallop, and severe dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 10–13%). In a middle-aged smoker with family history of coronary disease presenting in cardiogenic shock, the presentation mimics acute myocardial infarction or fulminant myocarditis. The clinical challenge is recognizing secondary arboviral reinfection causing severe transient dilated cardiomyopathy and capillary leak shock.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is set on Day 1 in the emergency department after fluid resuscitation, physical examination (hypotension, fever, fine crackles, S3 gallop), initial laboratory testing (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated BNP, stable mild cardiac biomarker elevation), ECG (sinus rhythm, frequent PVCs), chest radiography (cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, effusions), and urgent bedside echocardiogram (EF 10%, global LV dilation without regional wall motion abnormalities), strictly prior to Day 3 seroconversion, DEN-3 RT-PCR, and cardiac catheterization.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute myocardial infarction / ischemic cardiomyopathy is excluded by lack of ST elevation, global rather than segmental wall motion abnormalities, non-rising cardiac enzymes, and angiographically normal coronaries. Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis or septic shock is excluded by negative blood cultures, low-level stable cardiac enzymes, and specific serological/molecular confirmation of secondary dengue serotype 3 infection.
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old male with a medical history of essential hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, profound fatigue, and progressive shortness of breath. One week prior, he developed high-grade fevers accompanied by generalized myalgias, frontal headache, and weakness. Three days ago, he developed exertional dyspnea that worsened progressively, associated with mild paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and orthopnea. He reports frequent lightheadedness and experienced one episode of coffee-ground emesis on the day of presentation. He denies chest pain, palpitations, cough, syncope, hematochezia, or hematuria. He is an active one-pack-per-day cigarette smoker with a family history of myocardial infarction in his father at age 77. He notes a recent sick contact with a brother who suffered an acute febrile illness 3 weeks earlier. Review of his records shows a prior hospitalization one year ago for an acute febrile illness accompanied by vague chest discomfort, transient T-wave inversions, and mildly elevated cardiac enzymes, which resolved completely with normal follow-up echocardiography (ejection fraction 58%).

On physical examination, the patient is lethargic, anxious, and diaphoretic. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 89/52 mmHg, temperature of 103°F (39.4°C), heart rate of 116 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 19 breaths per minute. Chest auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds at both lung bases with scattered bilateral fine crackles. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal S1 and S2 heart sounds with an audible S3 gallop; no murmurs, rubs, or clicks are present. There is no peripheral edema, cyanosis, jaundice, or rash.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a leukocyte count of 3,100 /uL, platelet count of 127,000 /uL, and hemoglobin of 12.0 g/dL. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is markedly elevated at 1,040 pg/mL. Cardiac enzymes demonstrate mild initial elevation. Electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventricular contractions and no ischemic ST-segment or T-wave changes. Plain chest radiography reveals cardiomegaly, bilateral interstitial pulmonary edema, and bilateral pleural effusions. Urgent bedside transthoracic echocardiography reveals severe global left ventricular dilation with an ejection fraction of 10% and absence of focal wall motion defects or focal thinning.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In a middle-aged smoker with family history of premature CAD presenting in cardiogenic shock with an S3 gallop and severely reduced ejection fraction (10%), acute myocardial infarction was an immediate concern. However, ECG lacked ischemic ST deviations, echocardiography showed global dilation without regional wall motion abnormalities, cardiac enzymes were only mildly elevated without typical rise-and-fall kinetics, and cardiac catheterization revealed normal coronaries.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Routine EKG was done which showed sinus rhythm and frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVC) with no ST or T wave ischemic changes

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Fulminant viral myocarditis (e.g., enterovirus, adenovirus) or septic shock
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute biventricular decompensation and cardiovascular collapse after a febrile prodrome can represent fulminant myocarditis or severe bacterial sepsis. However, blood cultures were sterile, and acute fulminant necrosis was ruled out because cardiac biomarkers remained stable and low over the course of hospitalization despite marked ventricular dilatation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Fulminant myocarditis with acute myocardial failure was ruled out as cardiac enzymes were almost normal in the setting of dilated cardiac chambers on Echo.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when acute serologic and molecular testing—heralded by baseline IgG positivity, Day 3 IgM seroconversion, and RT-PCR positive for dengue virus serotype 3 (DEN-3)—confirmed severe secondary dengue infection complicated by acute dilated cardiomyopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Anti-dengue IGM by ELISA was negative at the time of admission but was positive for IGG antibodies at that time. Repeat testing on day 3 showed positive IGM antibodies for dengue. The diagnosis was confirmed with reverse transcriptase polymerised chain reaction (RT-PCR) which was positive for dengue virus serotype 3 (DEN-3). In view of above clinical scenario with positive dengue serology, history of myocarditis during primary dengue infection 1 year ago, and echocardiographic findings, diagnosis of dengue virus induced dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) was made.

editor_comments: Meticulous admission breakpoint formulation. Zero pathogen leakage. Thorough clinical differential addressing cardiogenic shock.
